The core idea revolves around inferring internal sensory states—specifically color perception—through external behavioral indicators. The sensory discrimination operator models how an agent learns to distinguish between stimuli, using a Yerkes-Watson-style apparatus where choices reflect discrimination ability. This leads to a probabilistic framework in GSI, where each trial contributes to posterior belief over color categories. The color dimensionality analysis extends this by proposing that hue, saturation, and lightness form independent axes, enabling structured inference. Behavioral conditional learning ties these together through reinforcement, forming a dynamic system where prior beliefs evolve with new evidence. These primitives collectively support a dual-mode reasoning process: one rooted in empirical observation and another in theoretical abstraction.
